opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really significant commitment, and honestly, it's the kind of thing that I don't think any other lab had done at the time. Dedicating 20% of the compute we've secured to date to alignment over the next four years is a big deal. Compute is one of the scarcest and most valuable resources at a lab like OpenAI, so putting a substantial chunk of it toward this problem sends a clear signal that the leadership takes it seriously.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. Compute alone doesn't solve alignment. The bottleneck has often been ideas, the right research directions, and people who can execute on them. What the commitment does is remove one potential excuse. If we have good ideas, we won't be stuck waiting in line for GPUs. And many of the approaches we're most excited about, like using AI systems to help with alignment research, scalable oversight, automated interpretability, and stress-testing our techniques with adversarial setups, are going to be very compute-intensive. So it matters that the resources are there.

I'd also say it's a bet. We set an ambitious goal: solving the core technical challenges of superintelligence alignment in four years. I'm not certain we'll succeed. But I think it's the right kind of goal to have, because if you aim for something modest, you'll get modest results. The compute commitment is part of what makes the ambition credible rather than just aspirational.

And finally, I hope it sets a precedent. Ideally other labs would look at this and think, "We should be making similar commitments." Alignment shouldn't be an afterthought you fund with leftovers. It should scale with capabilities, and this is one concrete step in that direction.

r001.rationale: The response says compute will go toward alignment, but it does not clarify that the commitment extends beyond Jan Leike’s team.

r002.rationale: It discusses the commitment’s significance and ambition, but does not use prior alignment investments as a benchmark.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison with previous alignment investment and does not state a threefold or greater increase.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we launched the Superalignment team, OpenAI committed 20% of the compute it had secured to date to this effort over the next four years. And I think that's a really big deal. If you look at what that number actually means, it's the single largest investment in alignment research that anyone has made so far. And that was something I really pushed for, because I think it's important that this isn't just a small side project — it needs to be a serious bet.

The way I think about it is: a lot of the alignment research that I'm most excited about is fundamentally compute-bound. If you want to do things like scalable oversight experiments, or automated interpretability where you're using models to explain what other models are doing, or run the kinds of evaluations where you deliberately train deceptively misaligned models to see whether your techniques catch them — those all require running a lot of large models. So having access to a serious amount of compute is really what makes it possible to do empirical alignment research at the frontier, rather than just on toy problems.

And then the other piece is that the ultimate goal here is to build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher. Once you have that, you can turn compute into alignment progress much more directly. You can run thousands of copies working on the problem, and so the compute commitment also matters a lot for that endgame.

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell it. 20% is a lot, but it's also not a guarantee that we'll solve the problem. The commitment is about resources, and resources are necessary but not sufficient. The thing I'm actually uncertain about is whether we have the right ideas, and whether we can make the research go fast enough. But at least now, when people ask "is OpenAI really taking this seriously?", I can point to something concrete. I think this is the kind of thing where you should hold us accountable: if in four years we haven't made real progress, that's a legitimate thing to criticise.

r001.rationale: It says the compute was committed to the effort when the Superalignment team launched, but does not clarify that the allocation extends beyond that team.

r002.rationale: It calls the commitment the largest alignment investment anyone had made, but does not use OpenAI’s prior alignment investments as the benchmark.

r003.rationale: It describes the commitment as large but gives no comparison with OpenAI’s previous alignment investment or threefold increase.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that it makes alignment a concrete priority. If you want to align systems that are much more capable than we are, you need to be able to run experiments with capable models, train new systems, and test whether your methods actually work. That takes compute.

But compute is an input, not a guarantee of success. You still need good research ideas, people who can execute on them, and ways to tell whether you’re making progress. In particular, you need evaluations that distinguish a system that reliably follows your intentions from one that just looks good in the situations you’ve tested.

So I’d view the commitment as creating an opportunity to do the work at the scale it needs. The harder question is whether we can turn those resources into convincing evidence that our alignment methods will continue to work as systems become more capable.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison with prior alignment investment or claim that the commitment exceeds it by more than threefold.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between committing compute and actually turning that compute into progress on alignment. Having substantial resources available matters, because it lets you test ideas at a scale where the problems you care about start to appear. But you also need good research directions, people who can execute on them, and a way to tell whether your methods are actually working.

So I’d view the commitment as an enabling condition, rather than evidence that alignment will be solved. Ultimately, the question is whether we can use those resources to get reliable evidence that increasingly capable systems will behave as intended.
